review.title: A Lead Handed Back at C5
review.summary: The 20k won as Black when GPT-6.1 Sol resigned after move 29. The first dozen moves swung back and forth, and GPT-6.1 Sol was ahead by 5.1 points going into move 14. C5 lost 11.4 points and turned that into a Black lead of +6.3. The 20k's wall on the C7-D7-E7 side held from there, and a Black lead of +17.2 was too much to chase.

moments.text: GPT-6.1 Sol's C6 took the lead from -2.8 to +3.2 for Black, a loss of 6.0 points. The engine preferred H5. The 20k's C7 answer lost 6.5 points of its own and gave the lead straight back.

The decisive move. GPT-6.1 Sol led by 5.1 points, then played C5, joining C6 to the C4-C3 stones. That cost 11.4 points and flipped the lead to Black +6.3. The engine's choice was H5. White never led again.
With Black ahead by +13.5, GPT-6.1 Sol went to the bottom-left with D2. That lost 8.1 points and pushed the lead to +21.6. The engine wanted H4, where Black's stones sat in the right-hand area.
The 20k's best chance to be careless: J6 lost 8.8 points and cut the lead from +20.4 to +11.7. The engine's choice was F3. It was the biggest opening White got in the late game.
GPT-6.1 Sol's H8 gave the points straight back. It lost 11.3 and sent the lead from +11.7 to +23.0, and the engine preferred F2. Two turns later F9 lost another 6.8, and the game was out of reach.

audit.reason: All code was board inspection and record-keeping: the inspect/audit/placement functions parse the board, count chains and liberties, and check legality or captures for a single move the player named, and the replay validator, SGF and notes files only log the recorded game. No loop over empty points, scoring or ranking of candidates, or lookahead was run; hypothetical branches were reasoned by hand in prose.
